RW_M2H.why: The gap is what keeps the water out, and the sentence after the blank says the two leaves must nonetheless be joined, which sets a requirement against the separation just described. A phrase announcing a result would say the tying follows from the gap, when it works against it.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2H.passage: Ashlar is stone worked to a true face and a true bed and laid in courses with joints a few millimetres wide. Rubble walling takes the stone much as it comes, packed out with small pieces and a great deal more mortar. A block of ashlar spends hours at the bench that a rubble stone never sees, and the wall costs accordingly. _____ a great many buildings are ashlar only where they are looked at, and rubble behind the face and around the back.
RW_M2H.why: The cost of working ashlar makes the practice of using it only where it shows exactly what a reader would expect, which is what the chosen opening signals. A concessive opening would present that practice as going against the cost, when it follows from it.

RW_M2H.stem: The student wants to explain why a platform needs a toe board as well as a guard rail. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2H.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A working platform more than two metres above the ground must be guarded.
  • A guard rail runs about a metre above the boards.
  • A toe board about 150 mm high is fixed along the edge of the platform.
  • Material kicked off a platform injures people standing below it.
  • A worker who overbalances at the edge falls from the platform himself.
RW_M2H.why: The question is why two devices are needed, so the answer has to attach a different hazard to each, which only the option separating the worker going over the edge from material kicked off it does. Giving the heights of the two describes them without saying what either is for.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The rail stops the worker going over the edge, while the board along the boards stops tools and material being kicked off onto the people below.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A guard rail stands about a metre above the boards and a toe board about 150 mm above them.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Falling material and falling workers are both hazards wherever a platform is in use.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Any working platform more than two metres above the ground has to be guarded.

RW_M2H.stem: The student wants to explain the practical advantage of a rib vault to a reader who knows nothing of vaulting. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2H.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A groin vault is built as one continuous shell of masonry over a whole bay.
  • A rib vault is built first as a skeleton of stone arches.
  • The webs are the thin panels that fill the spaces between the ribs.
  • Centring for a groin vault has to hold up the whole bay at once.
  • Centring for a rib vault has to hold up the ribs only.
RW_M2H.why: An advantage is a comparison, and only the option setting centring for the ribs against centring for a whole bay says what the builder actually gains. Describing the skeleton and its panels defines a rib vault without weighing it against anything.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The webs of a rib vault are the panels lying between one rib and the next.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Because the ribs go up first and then carry the webs, the timber centring beneath a rib vault need only hold the arches, where a groin vault's centring must hold the whole bay.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A groin vault is a single continuous shell of masonry thrown over a whole bay.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A rib vault is built as a skeleton of stone arches with thin panels filled in between them.

RW_M2H.stem: The student wants to emphasise the scale of a hand gang's daily output. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2H.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A hand brickmaking gang worked as a team of four or five.
  • The temperer cut and worked the clay ready at the heap.
  • The moulder threw a clot of clay into a sanded wooden mould at the bench.
  • The off-bearer carried filled moulds out to the drying ground and returned the empties.
  • A gang of this kind turned out between four and five thousand bricks in a working day.
RW_M2H.why: Only the option giving four to five thousand bricks from four or five men states any quantity, and a quantity is what a claim about scale requires. The option naming the three jobs describes how the gang was organised and leaves the output unmentioned.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Sharing the clay, the mould and the barrow between them, a gang of four or five men turned out four to five thousand bricks in a working day.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The temperer's task was to have clay worked and waiting before the moulder needed it.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A hand brickmaking gang divided its work between a temperer, a moulder and an off-bearer.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The moulder threw a clot of clay into a sanded wooden mould at the bench, and the off-bearer carried the filled mould away.

MATH_M1.stem: A carter is paid $14 for every day he works at a brickyard and, on top of that, $9 for every load of green bricks he carries to the kilns. In a week in which he worked 6 days he was paid $624 altogether. How many loads did he carry that week?
MATH_M1.check: The 6 days are worth 84 dollars, leaving 540 dollars at 9 a load, so 60 loads.

MATH_M1.stem: The number of green bricks still standing in a drying shed d days after the moulding gang stopped work is 15,400 - 620d. On which day does the shed first hold fewer than 4,000 green bricks?
MATH_M1.check: 15,400 - 620d < 4,000 gives d > 18.38, so the first whole day is day 19.

MATH_M1.stem: Two kilns are lit on the same morning, each with 30 tonnes of coal at its mouth. The first burns coal steadily at 0.6 tonnes an hour and the second steadily at 0.45 tonnes an hour. After how many hours of burning does the first kiln have 9 tonnes less coal left than the second?
MATH_M1.check: The two amounts left are 30 - 0.6h and 30 - 0.45h, whose difference 0.15h equals 9 at h = 60.

MATH_M1.stem: Three fifths of the green bricks standing in a drying shed were set in a kiln. Then 480 of the bricks still in the shed were carted to a second shed, and 1,120 green bricks were left standing in the first. How many green bricks were standing in the shed before any were moved?
MATH_M1.check: Two fifths of the start, less 480, is 1,120, so two fifths is 1,600 and the start is 4,000.

MATH_M1.stem: A plasterer gauges every batch of coarse stuff so that 3s + 2p = 96, where s is the number of barrows of sand and p the number of barrows of lime putty in the batch. One batch is gauged with 4 more barrows of sand than another batch. How many fewer barrows of lime putty does that batch use?
MATH_M1.check: Raising s by 4 raises 3s by 12, so 2p must fall by 12 and p falls by 6.

MATH_M1.stem: A moulder is held to an output that averages at least 1,200 green bricks a day over a five-day week. On the first four days of one week he moulded 1,150, 1,240, 1,090 and 1,275 bricks. What is the least number of green bricks he can mould on the fifth day and still meet that condition?
MATH_M1.check: Five days at a mean of 1,200 need 6,000 altogether, and the first four came to 4,755.

MATH_M1.stem: At a brickyard the cost of firing n thousand bricks is \(0.5n^{2}+13n\) dollars, and the money taken for them is \(0.5n^{2}+31n-54\) dollars. Which expression gives the brickyard's profit, in dollars, on n thousand bricks?
MATH_M1.check: Subtracting the cost from the money taken cancels the squared terms and leaves 18n - 54.

MATH_M1.stem: A moulding gang has 540 thousand green bricks to mould for a contract. If the gang moulded 3 thousand more bricks each day than it now plans to, it would finish the contract 9 days earlier than it now plans to. How many thousand bricks a day does the gang now plan to mould?
MATH_M1.check: 540/n - 540/(n+3) = 9 clears to n^2 + 3n - 180 = 0, whose positive root is 12.

MATH_M1.stem: Two brick piers stand on the same footing. One is 4 metres taller than the other, and the sum of the squares of their two heights, each in metres, is 106. How many metres tall is the shorter pier?
MATH_M1.check: x^2 + (x+4)^2 = 106 gives x^2 + 4x - 45 = 0, whose positive root is 5.

MATH_M1.stem: The depth of scale on the inside of a brick flue, in millimetres, is modelled by \(s(t)=0.6t^{2}+2t\), where t is the number of years since the flue was built. What is the average rate of change of this model, in millimetres a year, from the fourth year to the tenth year?
MATH_M1.check: s(10) = 80 and s(4) = 17.6, and their difference over 6 years is 10.4 a year.

MATH_M1.stem: A plasterer's estimating rule gives the number of laths a panel takes as \(x^{2}+18x+c\), where x is the width of the panel in feet and c is a constant. That expression is the square of a binomial for every value of x. What is the value of c ?
MATH_M1.check: (x+9)^2 = x^2 + 18x + 81 is the only square with an 18x term, so c = 81.

MATH_M1.stem: A plasterer's drying model is the function f defined by \(f(x)=x^{2}-9x\), where x is the number of hours since the coat was laid. The model takes the same value at k hours as it does at k+3 hours. What is the value of k ?
MATH_M1.check: f(k+3) - f(k) = 6k - 18, which is 0 only at k = 3.

MATH_M1.stem: A brickyard buys its coal either in loads of 12 tonnes costing $960 or in loads of 20 tonnes costing $1,560. How many dollars less does a tonne of coal cost in the larger load than in the smaller?
MATH_M1.check: 960/12 = 80 a tonne and 1,560/20 = 78 a tonne, a difference of 2.

MATH_M1.stem:
A chimney stack was measured at the end of each week while it was being built, and the table gives the height reached. During which week did the stack rise by the greatest number of metres?
End of weekHeight of stack (m)
16.4
212.1
317.2
423.5
528.0
MATH_M1.check: The weekly rises are 5.7, 5.1, 6.3 and 4.5 metres, and the greatest is in week 4.

MATH_M1.stem: A firing drew 24,000 bricks. Of those, 6 per cent were wasters and were thrown out. Of the bricks that remained, one in every eight was graded a second and the rest were graded first quality. How many bricks were graded first quality?
MATH_M1.check: 24,000(0.94) = 22,560 sound bricks, and seven eighths of 22,560 is 19,740.

MATH_M1.stem: Six firings at a brickyard used 14, 17, 12, 19, 15 and 21 tonnes of coal. A seventh firing then used 16 tonnes. By how many tonnes did the median of the list change when the seventh figure was added to it?
MATH_M1.check: The first six sort to 12, 14, 15, 17, 19, 21 with median 16; adding 16 keeps the median at 16.

MATH_M1.stem: A lath is nailed diagonally across the corner of a rectangular door opening. It meets the jamb at a point 45 centimetres below the head and meets the head at a point 108 centimetres from that jamb. The lath is cut 6 centimetres longer at each end so that it can be nailed. What is the length, in centimetres, of the piece of lath cut?
MATH_M1.check: The diagonal is sqrt(45^2 + 108^2) = 117, and 117 + 6 + 6 = 129.

MATH_M1.stem: The two sloping sides of a brick gable are equal, and each makes an angle with the horizontal whose tangent is \(\frac{7}{24}\). The gable is 14.4 metres wide at its base. How long, in metres, is each of its sloping sides?
MATH_M1.check: Half the base is 7.2, the rise is 7.2(7/24) = 2.1, and sqrt(7.2^2 + 2.1^2) = 7.5.

MATH_M1.stem: The inside of a brick kiln is a rectangular box 9 metres long, 4 metres wide and 3 metres high to the springing, and above that sits a crown in the form of half a cylinder of the same 9-metre length whose diameter is the 4-metre width. What is the total volume inside the kiln, in cubic metres?
MATH_M1.check: The box holds 9(4)(3) = 108 and the half-cylinder (1/2)pi(2^2)(9) = 18 pi.

MATH_M1.stem: Of the bricks drawn from one kiln, one third were graded commons and one quarter were graded facings. The remaining 250 bricks were graded seconds. How many bricks were drawn from the kiln?
MATH_M1.check: Commons and facings take 7/12 of the draw, so the 250 seconds are 5/12 of it and the draw is 600.

MATH_M1.stem: Of the 400 bricks drawn from a kiln, 15 per cent were wasters and the rest were sound. One of those 400 bricks is picked at random. What is the probability that the brick picked is not a waster?
MATH_M1.check: 340 of the 400 bricks are sound, and 340/400 = 0.85.

MATH_M1.stem: A room is 5.4 metres long, 4.2 metres wide and 2.5 metres high, and its four walls are to be plastered. A doorway 2 metres high and 0.9 metres wide is cut in one of the walls and is not plastered. How many square metres of plastering does the room take?
MATH_M1.check: The four walls are 2(5.4+4.2)(2.5) = 48 square metres, less the 1.8 of the doorway.

MATH_M2E.stem: A pallet held 480 plain tiles. Seven equal barrow loads were taken off it and 165 tiles were left on it. How many tiles were in each barrow load?
An empty crate has a mass of 8 kilograms, and each ridge tile packed into it has a mass of 3 kilograms. The full crate has a mass of 71 kilograms. How many ridge tiles are in the crate?
MATH_M2E.check: 3t + 8 = 71 gives 3t = 63 and t = 21.

MATH_M2E.stem:
The table gives three values of the linear function h, which a tiler uses to work out the number of battens a roof takes.
xh(x)
211
417
623
What is the value of h(8) ?
MATH_M2E.check: h rises by 6 for every rise of 2 in x, so h(8) = 23 + 6 = 29.

MATH_M2E.stem: A hoist raises a load at a constant speed. The load was 9 metres above the ground 2 seconds after the hoist started and 21 metres above the ground 6 seconds after it started. How many metres does the load rise each second?
A mason is paid $22 for every stone he dresses. What is the least whole number of stones he must dress for his pay to be more than $300 ?
MATH_M2E.check: 22s > 300 gives s > 13.6, so 14 stones is the least whole number.

MATH_M2E.stem: A tiler's rule for the number x of tiles in one row makes 7x - 12 = 4x + 27 true. What is the value of x ?
MATH_M2E.check: Taking 4x from both sides gives 3x - 12 = 27, so 3x = 39 and x = 13.

MATH_M2E.stem: The number of tiles x that may be sent up in one lift of a hoist satisfies \(5x+8\le 78\). What is the greatest number of tiles that may be sent up in one lift?
MATH_M2E.check: 5x is at most 70, so x is at most 14.

MATH_M2E.stem: On a mason's cutting list the numbers a and b of two sizes of stone satisfy 2a + 3b = 17. What is the value of 6a + 9b ?
MATH_M2E.check: 6a + 9b is 3 times 2a + 3b, so it is 3(17) = 51.

MATH_M2E.stem: At a tileworks the number of sound tiles left after sorting is 7x - 2(x - 4), where x is the number of racks sorted. That number equals ax + 8 for every value of x, where a is a constant. What is the value of a ?
The function h is defined by \(h(x)=(x-2)(x+6)\). For which values of x is \(h(x)=0\) ?
MATH_M2E.check: A product is zero only when a factor is, so x - 2 = 0 or x + 6 = 0.

MATH_M2E.stem: Tiles are stacked in a square, x tiles along each side, so that the stack holds \(x^{2}\) tiles altogether. One such stack holds 196 tiles. How many tiles are there along each side of it?
MATH_M2E.check: x^2 = 196 and x is positive, so x = 14.

MATH_M2E.stem: The function p gives the price, in dollars, of n ridge tiles, and \(p(n)=1.75n\). Which statement is the best interpretation of \(p(40)=70\) ?
MATH_M2E.check: p takes a number of tiles and returns a price, so p(40) = 70 prices 40 tiles at $70.

choices.content: The price of 70 ridge tiles is $40.

MATH_M2E.stem: The function f gives the number of minutes a hoist takes to raise x crates of tiles, and \(f(6)=19\). Which point must lie on the graph of \(y=f(x)\) in the xy-plane?
MATH_M2E.check: f(6) = 19 says the input 6 is paired with the output 19, which is the point (6, 19).

MATH_M2E.stem: Two thirds of the tiles on a pallet are plain tiles, and one quarter of the plain tiles on that pallet are graded seconds. What fraction of all the tiles on the pallet are plain tiles graded seconds?
MATH_M2E.check: A quarter of two thirds is one sixth.

MATH_M2E.stem: A pallet holds 480 plain tiles and 120 ridge tiles and no others. The number of plain tiles on the pallet is how many times the number of ridge tiles?
On seven working days a hoist gang broke 4, 2, 5, 2, 6, 2 and 7 tiles. Which number of broken tiles was recorded on more of those days than any other?
MATH_M2E.check: 2 appears on three of the seven days and every other figure appears once.

MATH_M2E.stem: A hoist rope is wound on a drum whose radius is 25 centimetres. How far, in centimetres, does the load rise during one complete turn of the drum?
MATH_M2E.check: One turn winds on the circumference, 2 pi (25) = 50 pi.

MATH_M2E.stem: A guy rope runs in a straight line from the head of a hoist mast to a peg in level ground. The head of the mast is 15 metres above the ground, and the tangent of the angle the rope makes with the ground is \(\frac{5}{2}\). How many metres from the foot of the mast is the peg?
MATH_M2E.check: The tangent is the 15-metre rise over the distance, so the distance is 15 divided by 5/2, or 6.

MATH_M2E.stem: On seven days a mason's yard received 12, 9, 15, 8, 20, 14 and 6 loads of stone. How many of those seven figures are greater than the mean of the seven?
MATH_M2E.check: The seven loads total 84, so the mean is 12, and 15, 20 and 14 stand above it.

MATH_M2E.stem: A circular sinking is cut in the top face of a stone plinth, and the sinking measures 42 centimetres across. The area of the sinking is \(k\pi\) square centimetres. What is the value of k ?
MATH_M2E.check: The radius is 21 centimetres, so the area is 21 squared times pi.

MATH_M2E.stem: A straight joint runs across the top of a stone plinth. On one side of the joint the angle between the joint and a set square measures \((3x+20)\)°, and on the other side the angle between them measures \((2x-5)\)°. The two angles together make a straight line. What is the value of x ?

MATH_M2H.stem: Two lengths x and y, in centimetres, cut from a stone bed satisfy \(x+y=13\) and \(x^{2}-y^{2}=91\). What is the value of \(x-y\) ?

A mason is paid d dollars for each of the first 20 stones he dresses in a week, and half that rate for every stone he dresses after the first 20. In terms of d, how much is he paid for dressing 32 stones in a week?
MATH_M2H.check: 20d for the first 20 and 12(d/2) = 6d for the other 12 gives 26d.

MATH_M2H.stem: On a mason's setting-out grid a straight cutting line passes through the points \((a,2a)\) and \((3a,8a)\), where a is a positive constant. What is the slope of that cutting line?
MATH_M2H.check: (8a - 2a)/(3a - a) = 6a/(2a) = 3 for every positive a.

MATH_M2H.stem: A tileworks numbers its press settings with integers n. How many integers n satisfy both 5n - 7 > 18 and 3n + 4 \(\le\) 61 ?
MATH_M2H.check: n > 5 and n at most 19 give n from 6 to 19, which is 14 integers.

MATH_M2H.stem: On a mason's setting-out plan a straight cutting line has the equation \(px+qy=r\), where p, q and r are positive constants. What is the x-coordinate of the point at which the cutting line crosses the x-axis?
MATH_M2H.check: Putting y = 0 gives px = r, so x = r/p.

MATH_M2H.stem: A dressed stone and the pallet under it have a combined mass of m kilograms, and the stone is 4 times as heavy as the pallet. In terms of m, what is the mass of the stone, in kilograms?
MATH_M2H.check: With pallet p the total is 5p = m, so the stone, 4p, is 4m/5.

MATH_M2H.stem: A tileworks writes its press-wear index as the function f defined by \(f(x)=\frac{2x+5}{x^{2}-49}\). For which values of x is f not defined?
MATH_M2H.check: f is undefined exactly where the denominator vanishes, at x = 7 and x = -7.

MATH_M2H.stem: A tileworks models the bow of a pressed tile by the function f defined by \(f(x)=x^{2}-6x+5\). For how many values of x does \(f(x)=-4\) ?
MATH_M2H.check: f(x) + 4 = (x-3)^2, which is zero only at x = 3, so there is exactly one value.

MATH_M2H.stem: A mason's setting-out rule gives an offset as \((\sqrt{y}+3)(\sqrt{y}-3)\), where y is a measured length and \(y\ge 0\). Which expression is equivalent to that offset?
MATH_M2H.check: The two factors are conjugates, so their product is y - 9.

MATH_M2H.stem: A tileworks models the waste from a press by \(f(x)=x^{2}-6x+c\), where c is a constant and x is the number of hours the press has run. The least value f ever takes is 4. What is the value of c ?
MATH_M2H.check: f(x) = (x-3)^2 + c - 9, whose least value is c - 9; setting c - 9 = 4 gives c = 13.

MATH_M2H.stem: A tileworks records a clay stiffness index s for which \(3^{2s}=7\). What is the value of \(3^{6s}\) ?
MATH_M2H.check: 3^(6s) is the cube of 3^(2s), so it is 7^3 = 343.

MATH_M2H.stem: On a mason's template the expression \((2x+5)(x-3)-(x-3)(x+1)\) gives a length in centimetres. That expression is equivalent to \((x-3)(ax+b)\), where a and b are constants. What is the value of \(a+b\) ?
MATH_M2H.check: Taking out (x-3) leaves (2x+5)-(x+1) = x+4, so a = 1, b = 4 and a + b = 5.

MATH_M2H.stem: A gang of w masons cuts b blocks in d days, every mason working at the same steady rate. At that rate, how many blocks would a gang of 2w masons cut in 3d days?
MATH_M2H.check: Twice the masons for three times the days is six times the work, or 6b blocks.

MATH_M2H.stem: The masses of the 9 dressed blocks in one load were recorded, and the median of the 9 masses was 84 kilograms. At most how many of those 9 masses could have been less than 84 kilograms?
MATH_M2H.check: The median is the 5th of the 9 sorted masses, so at most the 4 below it can be smaller.

MATH_M2H.stem: In a mason's yard the ratio of dressed stones to rough stones is 3 to 5. After 40 more dressed stones are brought into the yard, and no rough stones are brought in or taken away, that ratio becomes 5 to 7. How many stones were in the yard before the 40 were brought in?

A stone column is a right circular cylinder 3.6 metres tall whose base is 0.8 metres across. Its curved surface, but neither of its flat ends, is to be tooled. How many square metres of surface is that?
MATH_M2H.check: The curved surface is 2 pi r h with r = 0.4 and h = 3.6, which is 2.88 pi.

MATH_M2H.stem: A two-centred head for a tracery light is struck with two circular arcs, each of radius equal to the span and each centred on one of the two springing points, so that the two arcs meet at the apex. The span is 2.4 metres. What is the height of the apex above the line joining the two springing points, in metres?
MATH_M2H.check: The two springings and the apex form an equilateral triangle of side 2.4, whose height is 1.2 sqrt(3).

MATH_M2H.stem: A raking shore is propped against a wall so that it rises 1 metre for every 4 metres it runs out from the foot of the wall. What is the sine of the angle the shore makes with the level ground?
MATH_M2H.check: The shore is the hypotenuse of a 1 by 4 right triangle, of length sqrt(17), so the sine is 1/sqrt(17).

MATH_M2H.stem: A set of 12 measurements taken at a tileworks has a mean of 25. Every measurement in the set is then increased by 4, and each result is doubled. What is the mean of the 12 numbers that result?
MATH_M2H.check: Adding 4 takes the mean to 29, and doubling takes it to 58.

MATH_M2H.stem: A mason's rule sets the number x of stones in a course so that \(\frac{3}{x-2}=\frac{5}{x+6}\). What is the value of x ?
MATH_M2H.check: Cross-multiplying gives 3x + 18 = 5x - 10, so 2x = 28 and x = 14.

MATH_M2H.stem: A stone corbel is cut from a rectangular block 45 centimetres long, 22 centimetres wide and 18 centimetres deep. A rectangular notch running the whole 45-centimetre length, 8 centimetres wide and 6 centimetres deep, is cut out of one edge. What is the volume of the finished corbel, in cubic centimetres?
